Edward Sapir. An American linguist and anthropologist who pioneered the study of Native American languages and explored language's role in shaping thought and culture. He conducted the first comprehensive linguistic documentation of Nootka, Takelma, Navajo, and other Native American languages, creating rigorous morphological and phonetic analyses that set the standard for the field. He argued that every language has a unique genius or internal logic that shapes how speakers conceptualise the world, laying the groundwork for linguistic relativity. Sapir collaborated with his student Benjamin Lee Whorf on the relationship between language and thought, culminating in what became known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis. His approach was distinctive: he sought to understand language as embedded in culture and psychology, not as a discrete formal system, and in doing so bridged linguistics and anthropology in a new way. His career spanned both academic linguistics and applied work in Native American language preservation, emphasising the cultural urgency of documenting these languages before they disappeared. Through his work with Whorf and his foundational studies, Sapir helped establish the field of linguistic anthropology itself.
